segments.en: Imagine flying low over the Indian Ocean and seeing rings of turquoise and white scattered below like strings of pearls. These are the atolls of the Maldives, more than a thousand coral islands stretched out in a long chain.

Most islands rise only a metre or so above the sea, making this one of the lowest-lying countries on Earth. People here know the ocean intimately, and caring for the reefs and the shoreline matters deeply.
In fact, the English word atoll comes from Dhivehi, the local language. Dhivehi is written in its own script, called Thaana, which runs from right to left.
The capital, Malé, is a small island packed with colourful buildings and buzzing motorbikes. Its old Friday Mosque was built from blocks of coral stone, carved with delicate patterns.
The Maldives is a Muslim nation, and daily life follows the rhythm of prayer times. When you visit a local island, it is respectful to cover your shoulders and knees.
For centuries, Maldivians have caught tuna with a simple pole and line, one fish at a time, from wooden boats called dhoni. It is a skilled and careful way of fishing that protects the sea.
Breakfast is often mas huni, tuna mixed with grated coconut, onion and chilli, scooped up with warm flatbread called roshi. With afternoon tea come little savoury snacks known as hedhikaa.
Beneath the waves lies another world. In Hanifaru Bay, manta rays gather in great numbers to feed, and in South Ari Atoll you might swim alongside a gentle whale shark.
On some nights, tiny plankton glow blue along the shore, so it looks as if the waves are sprinkled with stars.
When the drums start, it is bodu beru, which means big drum. Men sing and drum faster and faster, until the dancers leap up and everyone is clapping along.
On local islands, children play football on sandy pitches, and neighbours chat in the shade on rope swing seats called joali. Everyone seems to know everyone.
Traders have sailed through these islands for a very long time, carrying cowrie shells gathered here, which were once used as money in markets across Asia and Africa.
As the sun sinks into the lagoon, it is time to sail on. To the northeast, Sri Lanka is waiting, with its tea hills and elephants.
